title: Knee Arthritis in Your 30s or 40s: Why It Happens and What You Can Do
metaDescription: Knee arthritis before 50: common causes (old injury, weight, family), what to do, and options such as realignment or a partial knee replacement.
intro: Knee arthritis can start before 50, usually after an old knee injury, or with extra weight, a family history, or another joint disease. It is not rare, and it is not a sign you did something wrong. Treatment is the same step-by-step plan, with extra care in deciding about surgery at a younger age.

sections.heading: Why do I have knee arthritis so young?
sections.body: The NHS and Versus Arthritis list the common reasons: a past knee injury or surgery, overusing a joint before it has healed, physically heavy work, being overweight, a family history, and other joint diseases such as gout or rheumatoid arthritis. Often more than one applies. Women are affected more often.

sections.heading: Is it really arthritis, or something else?
sections.body: Pain in younger people can also come from a torn cartilage pad (meniscus), a ligament injury or a problem under the kneecap. That is why examination matters. Sometimes an X-ray or scan is needed to be sure.

sections.heading: What should I do first?
sections.body: The same steps as at any age. Settle the pain with medicines, start exercises to strengthen the muscles around the knee, watch your weight, and add physiotherapy treatments if needed. Protect the knee from further injury, and see us again if symptoms change.

sections.heading: Are there operations that save the natural knee?
sections.body: Sometimes. The NHS describes osteotomy, where the shin bone is reshaped to move pressure off the worn part of the knee, for selected people. A knee replacement may still be needed later. The NHS lists keyhole washing-out as an option only for some people, and it is not usually helpful for general wear-type arthritis.

sections.heading: Can younger people have a knee replacement?
sections.body: Yes, if arthritis is severe and other treatment has not helped. A partial knee replacement can suit those whose arthritis affects only one part of the knee. Knee replacements typically last about 25 years, according to the NHS, so surgery at a young age may mean another operation later. We discuss that honestly so you can decide.

sections.heading: How do I protect my knees long term?
sections.body: Keep your weight healthy, keep the thigh muscles strong, avoid repeated heavy impact, and treat knee injuries properly instead of ignoring them.

faqs.q: What is the earliest age for knee arthritis?
faqs.a: It can occur in the 30s, especially after injury, though it is most common after 45.

faqs.q: Can a sports injury cause arthritis later?
faqs.a: Past knee injury is a recognised risk factor, so proper treatment of injuries matters.

faqs.q: Should I wait until I'm older for a knee replacement?
faqs.a: If it is possible to manage well without surgery, many people wait. If you cannot, there are options. We discuss both.

faqs.q: Is partial knee replacement better for young patients?
faqs.a: It can suit them when only one part of the knee is affected.

faqs.q: Can I play sport with early arthritis?
faqs.a: Low-impact sports are usually fine. Ask us about higher-impact ones.
